baselines.name: LM-only / unconstrained decoding
baselines.fair_comparison: Compared alongside constrained frameworks. The paper uses the same model within each experiment setup; it does not specify other matched hyperparameters.

baselines.name: Guidance
baselines.fair_comparison: For the open-source coverage comparison, use the same Llama-3.2-1B-Instruct model, prompt, greedy zero-temperature decoding, and one-run protocol. baselines.name: Outlines
baselines.fair_comparison: For the open-source coverage comparison, use the same Llama-3.2-1B-Instruct model, prompt, greedy zero-temperature decoding, and one-run protocol. For the llama.cpp efficiency comparison, use the same Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct model, backend, hardware, and batch size as the other engines in that experiment.

baselines.name: Llamacpp
baselines.fair_comparison: For the open-source coverage comparison, use the same Llama-3.2-1B-Instruct model, prompt, greedy zero-temperature decoding, and one-run protocol. In the main efficiency comparison, use the same Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct model, llama.cpp backend, hardware, and batch size as Guidance and Outlines.

baselines.name: XGrammar
baselines.fair_comparison: For the open-source coverage comparison, use the same Llama-3.2-1B-Instruct model, prompt, greedy zero-temperature decoding, and one-run protocol. Its llama.cpp efficiency comparison is not possible; the paper instead compares it with Guidance using Hugging Face Transformers.

baselines.name: OpenAI
baselines.fair_comparison: Compared on the schema benchmark, but its proprietary underlying model differs from the open-source engines’ Llama-3.2-1B-Instruct; the paper says those empirical-coverage results are not directly comparable.

baselines.name: Gemini
baselines.fair_comparison: Compared on the schema benchmark, but its proprietary underlying model differs from the open-source engines’ Llama-3.2-1B-Instruct; the paper says those empirical-coverage results are not directly comparable.

metrics.name: Declared coverage
metrics.caveat: It is not an estimate of true coverage; the paper treats it as an upper bound on empirical and true coverage and reports empirical coverage alongside it.

metrics.name: Empirical coverage
metrics.caveat: It checks compliance only for the finite outputs observed, so it approximates rather than establishes true coverage; it is also influenced by the LM and sampling method. The paper reports declared coverage and compliance rate alongside it.

metrics.name: JSON Schema Test Suite coverage
metrics.caveat: Test-suite performance does not straightforwardly correspond to empirical coverage: features are not equally represented in real-world schemas, and under-constraining can leave the LM to produce valid outputs despite insufficient constraints. The paper also reports over- and under-constrained failures.

metrics.name: Compilation errors, over-constrained failures, and under-constrained failures
metrics.caveat: The reported counts are categories with at least one occurrence; categories can have multiple failure types, so the columns need not sum to the total number of categories.

controls.name: LM-only / unconstrained reference
controls.detail: Run without constrained decoding alongside the constrained frameworks for efficiency, empirical coverage, and the reasoning-task accuracy comparisons.
controls.rules_out: Shows how the measured generation speed, schema compliance, or task accuracy compares with the same experiment’s unconstrained model condition; it does not isolate which part of a constrained framework causes a difference.

confounds.name: Efficiency differences may reflect engines processing schemas of different difficulty rather than engine speed
confounds.detail: An engine with lower schema coverage may only process simpler and shorter schemas, which can compile and generate faster and bias averages over each engine’s own covered instances.
confounds.ruled_out_by: Calculate efficiency metrics on the intersection of instances covered by all engines.

confounds.name: Empirical coverage may depend on the underlying LM or sampling method, not just the framework
confounds.detail: The paper explicitly notes that empirical coverage is influenced by the LM and sampling methods employed.
confounds.ruled_out_by: For the open-source framework comparison, hold the model and decoding setup fixed: Llama-3.2-1B-Instruct, greedy zero-temperature decoding, and one generation run. The paper cautions that OpenAI and Gemini results are not directly comparable because their underlying models differ.

confounds.name: An engine may appear empirically covered because the LM happens to produce valid outputs despite insufficient constraints
confounds.detail: Under-constraining can delegate responsibility to the LM, which may still produce valid output even when the engine would allow invalid instances.
confounds.ruled_out_by: On the official JSON Schema Test Suite, check both directions: require generation of valid instances and blocking of invalid instances, and report under-constrained failures.

confounds.name: Quality effects may be caused by inadequate prompting, context, or schema design rather than constrained decoding
confounds.detail: The paper cites the argument that earlier observed performance declines could result from inadequate prompting, insufficient context, or poorly crafted schemas.
confounds.ruled_out_by: Use the original prompt specifications from the cited setup and evaluate tasks with simple output structures designed to isolate constrained decoding’s effects on reasoning.

evidence_standards.name: Coverage decoding and timeout protocol
evidence_standards.detail: Empirical coverage uses greedy decoding at zero temperature and a single generation run. Apply a 40-second timeout to grammar compilation and another 40 seconds to generation; exceeding either is a schema processing failure.

evidence_standards.name: Efficiency summaries and setup
evidence_standards.detail: Report medians of the result samples. Use batch size 1 and a single NVIDIA A100-SXM4-80GB GPU with AMD EPYC 7543 CPU; measure on the intersection of instances covered by all engines. The paper does not state the number of samples or seeds.

evidence_standards.name: Quality scoring and trial reporting
evidence_standards.detail: Report task accuracy using case-sensitive exact match for Last Letter, exact match for Shuffle Objects, and number exact match for GSM8K. The paper does not state the number of runs, seeds, variance estimates, or a statistical test.

datasets.name: newstest2013
datasets.eval_protocol: English–German Pick-Revise evaluation; four simulated editing cycles, reporting BLEU. At each cycle, add a reference phrase of up to three words missing from the current hypothesis; test both strict (the complete phrase is missing) and relaxed (only the first word is missing) constraints.

datasets.name: newstest2014
datasets.eval_protocol: English–French Pick-Revise evaluation; four simulated editing cycles, reporting BLEU. At each cycle, add a reference phrase of up to three words missing from the current hypothesis; test both strict (the complete phrase is missing) and relaxed (only the first word is missing) constraints.

datasets.name: Autodesk Post-Editing corpus
datasets.eval_protocol: For terminology adaptation, divide the corpus into approximately 100,000 training sentences and 1,000 test segments. Extract source–target n-gram terminology candidates of lengths 2–5 from training data, retaining pairs with PMI ≥ 0.9 and each phrase occurring at least five times; constrain the target phrase when its source phrase occurs in a test segment. Report BLEU. Also use an Autodesk-derived test corpus for the English–Portuguese Pick-Revise evaluation, with four simulated editing cycles and strict and relaxed constraints.

baselines.name: Baseline
baselines.fair_comparison: Compare the baseline translation output with GBS on the same Autodesk test data; the baseline has no terminology constraints.

metrics.name: BLEU
metrics.caveat: A BLEU improvement could be due merely to the terminology appearing somewhere in the output rather than being placed reasonably; the paper also evaluates random insertion and prepending of terms.

controls.name: Baseline output without terminology constraints
controls.detail: The unmodified baseline translation output, with no terminology added.
controls.rules_out: That the reported gain is simply the baseline system's performance without the intervention.

controls.name: Random insertion
controls.detail: Insert terminology constraints at random positions in the baseline output.
controls.rules_out: That GBS's BLEU improvement is explained merely by the terms appearing somewhere in the output.

controls.name: Beginning
controls.detail: Prepend terminology constraints to the baseline translations.
controls.rules_out: That GBS's BLEU improvement is explained merely by adding the terms, rather than placing them through constrained decoding.

confounds.name: BLEU gains arise merely from terms appearing in the output, not reasonable placement
confounds.detail: The headline BLEU improvement could occur even if the terminology were inserted at arbitrary positions.
confounds.ruled_out_by: Evaluate random insertion and prepending of terms to baseline outputs alongside GBS.

confounds.name: The especially large English–Portuguese gain reflects its training-data/domain mismatch
confounds.detail: The authors say the large gain is probably due to this system's training data being very different from the IT domain.

evidence_standards.name: Beam size 10
evidence_standards.detail: The paper sets beamSize to 10 for all experiments; it reports no seeds, variance estimates, or statistical tests.

datasets.name: WMT’14 newstest2014 English–German
datasets.eval_protocol: Developer test version, 2,737 sentences. BLEU is computed on detokenized output with sacreBLEU (BLEU+case.mixed+lang.en-de+numrefs.1+smooth.exp+test.wmt14+tok.13a+v.1.2.6). Constraint experiments use reference-derived sets: rand1–rand4 select one to four random reference words, and phr4 selects a random four-word phrase; constraints are then BPE-processed.

baselines.name: Grid Beam Search (GBS)
baselines.fair_comparison: Simulated in the same framework on the same model, test set, and constraints. After BPE, sentences are grouped by constraint count C and decoded with beam b(C+1); the paper tests b=10, 5, and 1, and disables beam adjustment for GBS.

baselines.name: Unconstrained beam search
baselines.fair_comparison: Reported on the same test set and model as an unconstrained reference, with beam sizes including k=5, 10, and 20; the paper does not specify further matching details.

metrics.name: BLEU
metrics.caveat: BLEU gains might come from the mere presence of reference constraints increasing n-gram counts rather than correct placement; the paper also examines examples and compares relative locations of constraint starts in references and outputs (Pearson r=0.82 for phr3).

metrics.name: Model score (length-normalized log probability)
metrics.caveat: The paper notes that model score and BLEU can move in opposite directions; it reports both, including BLEU against model score as constraints are added.

controls.name: Unconstrained decoding
controls.detail: Decode the same test inputs without lexical constraints; unconstrained BLEU is reported alongside constrained results.
controls.rules_out: Provides a reference for whether constrained decoding changes scores relative to decoding without the intervention; it does not rule out gains caused merely by constraint-token presence.

confounds.name: BLEU gains reflect reference n-gram overlap from inserting constraints, not sensible placement
confounds.detail: Because constraints are selected from references, their appearance in outputs could raise BLEU even if the decoder places them incorrectly.
confounds.ruled_out_by: The paper examines output examples and compares the relative position of each constraint’s first word in reference and output; for phr3 it reports Pearson r=0.82.

confounds.name: Longer outputs explain the runtime increase without pruning
confounds.detail: The authors consider whether unpruned constrained decoding is slower because it produces longer outputs.
confounds.ruled_out_by: They measure mean output length and report it is roughly the same across constraint sets.

evidence_standards.name: Reported decoding and scoring setup
evidence_standards.detail: Unless otherwise noted, completed hypotheses are scored by dividing cumulative sentence score by word count, and threshold pruning removes hypotheses whose log probability is more than 20 below the best completed hypothesis. Decoding stops when all beam hypotheses are complete or maximum length N is reached. Experiments use a single Volta P100 GPU with no ensembling or batching; runtime is decoding-only and excludes model loading and setup. No seeds, variance estimates, or statistical tests are specified.

metrics.name: Triplet-based micro-precision
metrics.caveat: The paper notes that GenIE has higher precision but lower recall and misses many entities and relations; it reports recall and F1 alongside precision.

metrics.name: Triplet-based micro-recall
metrics.caveat: The paper reports precision and F1 alongside recall to show the precision–recall balance.

metrics.name: Bracketing F1-score
metrics.caveat: The paper observes that unconstrained LLaMA often produces invalid parse trees, so it reports parse-tree validity alongside F1.

metrics.name: Parse-tree validity
metrics.caveat: Validity does not measure parsing correctness; the paper reports bracketing F1 alongside it.

metrics.name: Per-token decoding latency (milliseconds/token)
metrics.caveat: Pure decoding latency is measured on an A100 GPU, while GCD overhead is measured on a consumer CPU; the paper reports them separately.

controls.name: Unconstrained decoding
controls.detail: Run the few-shot LLaMA models without grammar constraints alongside the constrained versions.
controls.rules_out: A difference is evidence for the effect of adding grammar-constrained decoding rather than merely using the same prompted model.

controls.name: Input-independent grammar (IIG)
controls.detail: Compare IIG with input-dependent grammar (IDG) for entity disambiguation and constituency parsing. For ED, IIG allows any entity in the catalog; for CP, its grammar can generate arbitrary-size trees with anonymized terminal nodes.
controls.rules_out: A difference is evidence for the contribution of input-dependent constraints relative to the paper's input-independent grammar condition.

confounds.name: IDG gains may come from repeating the input's left context, rather than from restricting output to input-specific candidates
confounds.detail: The paper notes that IDG forces the model to repeat left context, which may condition the model toward the correct entity independently of the narrower candidate set.
confounds.ruled_out_by: Not ruled out: the paper compares IDG with IIG but reports no measurement that isolates the effect of left-context repetition from candidate-set restriction.

evidence_standards.name: 90% confidence intervals
evidence_standards.detail: The results tables report 90% confidence intervals: cIE values include intervals, ED interval widths are stated as 0.1–0.3, and CP F1 interval widths are stated as 4.0–6.0. The paper does not specify the statistical test or a threshold for calling results ties.

evidence_standards.name: Few-shot demonstration count
evidence_standards.detail: Results are reported with 4 shots for cIE and ED, and 8 shots for constituency parsing.

datasets.name: JSON-mode-eval
datasets.eval_protocol: Used for JSON Schema and unconstrained JSON mask-generation evaluations; the unconstrained-JSON ablation measures average mask-generation time with Llama-3.1 8B. Also used for function-calling evaluation, where syntactic correctness is reported as accuracy. No split or item count is stated.

datasets.name: Synthetic dataset
datasets.eval_protocol: Used for XML and Python DSL mask-generation evaluations, and for XML code-generation evaluation; the latter reports syntactic correctness as accuracy with Llama-3.1 8B. No split or item count is stated.

baselines.name: Outlines (v1.0)
baselines.fair_comparison: For mask generation, evaluated with the other libraries on Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct using an AMD Ryzen 9 7950X CPU and NVIDIA RTX 4090 GPU. In end-to-end serving, SGLang + Outlines is compared with SGLang + XGrammar on the same serving engine.

baselines.name: llama.cpp grammar engine (b3998)
baselines.fair_comparison: For mask generation, evaluated with the other libraries on Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct using an AMD Ryzen 9 7950X CPU and NVIDIA RTX 4090 GPU. In end-to-end serving, the comparison uses Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct, JSON Schema and unconstrained JSON, online serving with fixed batch sizes, AMD EPYC 7R13 CPU and NVIDIA H100 GPU, and a fixed maximum output length.

baselines.name: lm-format-enforcer (v0.10.9)
baselines.fair_comparison: For mask generation, evaluated with the other libraries on Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct using an AMD Ryzen 9 7950X CPU and NVIDIA RTX 4090 GPU. The paper notes that this regex-based method does not support CFG.

baselines.name: vLLM with Outlines (v0.6.3)
baselines.fair_comparison: Compared for end-to-end serving using Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct, JSON Schema and unconstrained JSON, online serving with fixed batch sizes, AMD EPYC 7R13 CPU and NVIDIA H100 GPU, and a fixed maximum output length.

baselines.name: SGLang + Outlines
baselines.fair_comparison: Compared with SGLang + XGrammar on the same serving engine; the cross-model evaluation uses JSON Schema.

metrics.name: TPOT (time per output token)
metrics.caveat: The paper defines TPOT as reflecting the overhead of applying constraints during token generation; it does not state a caveat or a substitute metric.

controls.name: MLC-LLM without XGrammar
controls.detail: The paper measures TPOT with and without XGrammar on MLC-LLM using Llama-3.1 8B, for JSON Schema and CFG (JSON), at batch sizes 1 and 16.
controls.rules_out: Provides an unmodified-engine reference for estimating the serving overhead associated with enabling XGrammar.

controls.name: Generation without XGrammar
controls.detail: For function calling and XML code generation, the paper compares outputs with and without XGrammar using Llama-3.1 8B and reports syntactic-correctness accuracy.
controls.rules_out: Shows the difference in syntactic correctness against unconstrained generation.

controls.name: PDA baseline without optimizations
controls.detail: The ablation starts with a PDA parser without optimizations, generating each mask by checking the entire vocabulary, then progressively adds node merging, the adaptive token mask cache, rule inlining, and context expansion.
controls.rules_out: Provides an ablation reference for assessing the effect of the added optimization techniques on mask-generation time.

evidence_standards.name: Reported averages under specified evaluation settings; no inferential threshold stated
evidence_standards.detail: Mask-generation results are reported as per-token latency, and the ablation reports average mask-generation time. End-to-end serving reports TPOT in online serving with fixed batch sizes; the comparison fixes maximum output length, with average input length 139 tokens and generated output length 53 tokens. The paper does not state seed or run counts, variance or confidence intervals, statistical tests, or a margin for treating results as ties. Hardware and model are specified for the evaluations; the end-to-end baseline comparison uses AMD EPYC 7R13 CPU and NVIDIA H100 GPU.

datasets.name: Stack dataset (Java, Go, and SQL evaluation subsets)
datasets.eval_protocol: For each language, take the first 1,000 samples successfully parsed by the Lark parser. For mask correctness and overhead evaluation, use teacher forcing with the oracle next token at each decoding step; positive samples pass if not rejected and negative samples pass if rejected.

datasets.name: MaskBench (JSON Schemas)
datasets.eval_protocol: Retain schemas whose generated Lark grammar parses every conformant JSON instance and rejects every non-conformant instance; randomly sample 1,000 schemas. The resulting set has 1,337 positive and 2,072 negative samples, with at least one of each per schema. Mask evaluation uses teacher forcing; positives pass if not rejected and negatives pass if rejected.

datasets.name: Multilingual HumanEval (Go subset)
datasets.eval_protocol: Evaluate 160 Go samples using pass@k for k=1, 3, 5, 10, 20, and 50; pass@1 uses greedy decoding and k>1 uses sampling at temperature 1.0 without top-p or top-k filtering.

datasets.name: MBGP
datasets.eval_protocol: Evaluate 939 samples ported from the MBPP dataset from Python to Go, using pass@k for k=1, 3, 5, 10, 20, and 50; pass@1 uses greedy decoding and k>1 uses sampling at temperature 1.0 without top-p or top-k filtering.

datasets.name: McEval (Go subset)
datasets.eval_protocol: Evaluate 50 Go questions using pass@k for k=1, 3, 5, 10, 20, and 50; pass@1 uses greedy decoding and k>1 uses sampling at temperature 1.0 without top-p or top-k filtering.

datasets.name: JSON-Mode-Eval
datasets.eval_protocol: Use 100 instruction/schema/output samples, excluding sample 39. Replace the schemas for samples 19, 24, 27, 33, 45, and 72 with equivalent schemas supported by the grammar-generation script; for samples 1, 15, 22, 90, and 97, enforce only the JSON grammar. A generated output is correct only if it converts to a JSON object exactly matching the oracle answer; strip code-block markers from unconstrained outputs before checking. Report pass@k for k=1, 3, 5, 10, 20, and 50; pass@1 is greedy and k>1 uses temperature 1.0 without top-p or top-k filtering.

datasets.name: Spider development set
datasets.eval_protocol: Evaluate 1,034 text-to-SQL samples with prompts constructed as in Syncode and a SQL grammar fixed to support the NOT operator. Report execution accuracy, using greedy decoding to generate one SQL query per sample.

baselines.name: XGrammar
baselines.fair_comparison: Use the same evaluation samples and oracle sequences for mask evaluations; convert the Lark grammars to the baseline's grammar format. Experiments use one GPU and one CPU thread.

baselines.name: GreatGramma
baselines.fair_comparison: Use the same evaluation samples and oracle sequences for mask evaluations; convert the Lark grammars to the baseline's grammar format. Experiments use one GPU and one CPU thread.

baselines.name: Formatron
baselines.fair_comparison: Use the same evaluation samples and oracle sequences for mask evaluations; convert the Lark grammars to the baseline's grammar format. Experiments use one GPU and one CPU thread.

baselines.name: LLGuidance
baselines.fair_comparison: Use the same evaluation samples and oracle sequences for mask evaluations; convert the Lark grammars to the baseline's grammar format. Experiments use one GPU and one CPU thread. For end-to-end throughput, compare with PSC on the same models and batch sizes.

baselines.name: Standard (unconstrained decoding)
baselines.fair_comparison: For downstream comparisons, use the same models, decoding settings, and default prompts as grammar-constrained decoding.

metrics.name: Sample pass rate
metrics.caveat: Counts positive samples as passed when not rejected and negative samples as passed when rejected; PSC's remaining failures were attributed to the reused GreatGramma lexer, not PSC itself.

metrics.name: Average mask-computation overhead
metrics.caveat: Measures CPU mask-tensor computation per decoding step and excludes transferring the mask to the GPU and applying it to logits, which the paper says is the same across methods.

metrics.name: End-to-end throughput
metrics.caveat: Measures tokens processed per second including mask computation and model inference; the paper reports it alongside unconstrained decoding as a reference.

metrics.name: Break-even point
metrics.caveat: Defined as the decoding time needed for PSC to amortize its preprocessing time relative to LLGuidance when users preprocess themselves.

metrics.name: Runtime memory for the DFA and precomputed masks; disk space of preprocessing results

controls.name: Unconstrained decoding (Standard)
controls.detail: Run the same model without grammar constraints; for downstream comparisons use the same prompts and decoding settings. In throughput experiments it is also measured across the tested batch sizes.
controls.rules_out: Provides a no-constraint reference, so downstream changes or throughput costs can be compared against running the model without the intervention.

confounds.name: Different prefixes and sequence lengths could affect mask-computation comparisons
confounds.detail: The paper notes that context and generated sequence length can significantly affect mask computation, potentially making method timings unfair to compare.
confounds.ruled_out_by: For RQ1–RQ3, evaluate all methods with teacher forcing on the same oracle next token at each decoding step.

confounds.name: LLM sampling randomness could affect downstream results
confounds.detail: Stochastic generations could make apparent downstream differences dependent on sampling variation.
confounds.ruled_out_by: Use greedy decoding for pass@1 and 50 samples per question for pass@k where k>1; compare methods with the same decoding settings and default prompts.

confounds.name: Training-data leakage could affect downstream scores
confounds.detail: A model's exposure to evaluation examples could affect measured task performance.
confounds.ruled_out_by: Compare constrained and unconstrained decoding on the same model with the same decoding settings; the paper says this should limit effects on the relative improvement.

confounds.name: Results could depend on the grammar, tokenizer, or model size selected
confounds.detail: A narrow set of deterministic grammars, tokenization schemes, or model sizes could make the reported efficiency or throughput gains unrepresentative.
confounds.ruled_out_by: Use multiple model series with different vocabulary sizes and tokenization schemes, evaluate throughput on Qwen2.5 7B as well as smaller models, and restrict grammar comparisons to deterministic context-free grammars; the paper acknowledges that PSC's applicability beyond deterministic grammars is not established.

evidence_standards.name: Teacher-forced evaluation for RQ1–RQ3
evidence_standards.detail: Use oracle sequences and the oracle next token at every decoding step so methods see the same contexts and sequence lengths.

evidence_standards.name: Downstream decoding and sampling protocol
evidence_standards.detail: Use greedy decoding for pass@1; for pass@k with k>1, use sampling at temperature 1.0 without top-p or top-k filtering. The authors use 50 samples per question for k>1 to reduce variance and the same settings and prompts for constrained and unconstrained comparisons.

evidence_standards.name: Throughput evaluation settings
evidence_standards.detail: Report end-to-end throughput across batch sizes 1, 2, 4, …, 256, using one GPU and one CPU thread.

datasets.name: Illustrative Example 3 (binary-string grammar)
datasets.eval_protocol: Used as an illustrative benchmark; convergence plots show the first 75 iterations. The example uses the grammar from Fig. 1 and a model prompted to generate binary strings ending in 1; Mixtral-8x7B-Instruct-v0.1 at temperature 1 is stated to produce such strings about 90% of the time.

datasets.name: SLIA (strings with linear integer arithmetic)
datasets.eval_protocol: Randomly select 15 problems; use 3 in-context specification–solution examples in each prompt and provide the grammar as the GAD constraint. Run GCD and ASAp for 2,000 iterations/sample per problem. Evaluate distribution alignment and also report how often sampled programs solve the specification.

datasets.name: INV-BV (conditional inverse generation with bit-vector arithmetic; INV-BV4 in the results)
datasets.eval_protocol: Randomly select 15 problems; use 3 in-context specification–solution examples in each prompt and provide the grammar as the GAD constraint. Run GCD and ASAp for 2,000 iterations/sample per problem. Evaluate distribution alignment and also report how often sampled programs solve the specification.

datasets.name: Constituency parsing (CP)
datasets.eval_protocol: Randomly select 6 problems. The grammar constrains outputs to well-parenthesized parse trees for English sentences. Run GCD and ASAp for 2,000 iterations/sample per problem.

baselines.name: Grammar-constrained decoding (GCD; Transformers-CFG implementation)
baselines.fair_comparison: Run both GCD and ASAp on the same selected benchmarks for 2,000 iterations/sample; the paper uses Mistral-7B for evaluation of the structured-decoding tasks.

metrics.name: KL divergence, KL(tilde Q || P)
metrics.caveat: The paper notes that GCD can show better KL divergence by being biased toward the most likely outcome even when its empirical expectation is far from the target; it reports empirical expectations alongside KL.

metrics.name: Empirical expectations of tilde Q_GCD, tilde Q_ASAp, and P
metrics.caveat: The paper says there are too few CP points to draw conclusions; it also reports KL divergence and aggregate least-squares differences between method and P expectations.

metrics.name: Sum of least-squares differences between method expectations and P expectations
metrics.caveat: The paper cautions that there are too few CP points to draw conclusions; it reports the individual expectation comparisons as scatter plots as well.

metrics.name: Correct-solution frequency for SLIA and INV-BV

evidence_standards.name: 2,000 iterations/sample per benchmark
evidence_standards.detail: The paper compares GCD and ASAp after this sampling budget; it reports no seeds, variance estimates, statistical tests, or numerical threshold for calling a difference real.

evidence_standards.name: Sliding-window KL and cumulative expectation plots
evidence_standards.detail: KL is plotted in windows of 500 samples; expectation plots show the empirical expectation over the first i samples. The paper does not state a significance criterion.

datasets.name: Amazon CloudWatch Logs Insights Language (CWIL)
datasets.eval_protocol: 41,183 internal API calls (40,167 positive and 1,016 negative); five-fold cross-validation with stratified folds preserving positive/negative proportions. Train a grammar on four folds and evaluate it as an API-call classifier on the fifth; report precision and recall, then rotate folds.

datasets.name: Dynatrace Query Language (DQL)
datasets.eval_protocol: 1,723 internal API calls (1,369 positive and 354 negative); five-fold cross-validation with stratified folds preserving positive/negative proportions. Train a grammar on four folds and evaluate it as an API-call classifier on the fifth; report precision and recall, then rotate folds.

datasets.name: Datadog Search Syntax (DSS)
datasets.eval_protocol: 838 internal API calls (821 positive and 17 negative); five-fold cross-validation with stratified folds preserving positive/negative proportions. Train a grammar on four folds and evaluate it as an API-call classifier on the fifth; report precision and recall, then rotate folds.

datasets.name: 10 CloudWatch Logs Insights tasks (end-to-end benchmark)
datasets.eval_protocol: Ten real natural-language tasks based on analyses of Autogrammar logs. For each task, call each of six LMs 100 times under each agent condition; allow up to five attempts to satisfy the post-condition, then run the query through boto3 and count calls that succeed without errors or exceptions.

baselines.name: Arvada
baselines.fair_comparison: Evaluated on CWIL using five-fold cross-validation and averaged across folds, as for Autogrammar; its oracle classifications use the CloudWatch-team grammar. Not evaluated on DQL or DSS because no ground-truth grammar was available.

baselines.name: LM-0
baselines.fair_comparison: Uses Claude Opus 4.6 and the same evaluation procedure as Autogrammar for RQ1; prompted with the same documentation Autogrammar reads and the literal first sentence of Autogrammar’s agent prompt. Retries up to three times if the output does not parse as a Lark grammar.

baselines.name: LM-40
baselines.fair_comparison: Uses Claude Opus 4.6 and the same evaluation procedure as Autogrammar for RQ1; extends LM-0’s prompt with 20 positive and 20 negative examples and uses the same opening prompt sentence. Retries up to three times if the output does not parse as a Lark grammar.

baselines.name: No Feedback
baselines.fair_comparison: In the end-to-end task comparison, uses the same task-solving setup without a grammar-check post-condition; compared on the same tasks and with the same six LMs and 100 calls per LM per task.

baselines.name: CloudWatch-team maintained grammar (Existing)
baselines.fair_comparison: Used as the grammar in the same post-condition setup as the Autogrammar grammar and evaluated on the same tasks, LMs, and number of calls.

controls.name: No Documentation
controls.detail: Autogrammar configuration without actions that depend on documentation; includes the 120-minute bound.
controls.rules_out: Whether documentation is necessary for the observed grammar quality; differences from the bounded Performance configuration measure the effect of removing documentation.

controls.name: No Execution Data
controls.detail: Autogrammar configuration without actions that depend on execution data; includes the 120-minute bound.
controls.rules_out: Whether execution data is necessary for the observed grammar quality; differences from the bounded Performance configuration measure the effect of removing execution data.

controls.name: No Feedback
controls.detail: End-to-end query agent without a grammar-check post-condition.
controls.rules_out: Whether the end-to-end improvement occurs without grammar feedback; a difference supports an effect of adding the post-condition.

confounds.name: The learned grammar may cover only a subset of the DSL because the logs are biased or incomplete
confounds.detail: If the logs do not exercise the full DSL, the grammar could perform well on held-out log examples without generalizing to broader use.
confounds.ruled_out_by: The authors evaluate end-to-end performance on a separate set of ten real CloudWatch Logs Insights tasks. They note this mitigates the concern but does not establish representativeness for all agent usage.

confounds.name: The baseline performance gap may be due to the LM’s pretrained knowledge rather than Autogrammar’s contributions
confounds.detail: An LM could potentially generate a good grammar from documentation and examples without Autogrammar’s learning process.
confounds.ruled_out_by: Compare against LM-0 (documentation only) and LM-40 (documentation plus 20 positive and 20 negative examples) using Claude Opus 4.6 and the same grammar-evaluation procedure.

evidence_standards.name: Grammar-analysis cross-validation and variability
evidence_standards.detail: Use five-fold stratified cross-validation; report mean ± standard deviation. The paper does not specify a statistical test for every reported grammar-analysis comparison.

evidence_standards.name: Grammar-baseline significance testing
evidence_standards.detail: Compare precision using a two-proportion z-test and apply Holm–Bonferroni correction at α=0.05 to control the family-wise false-positive rate.

evidence_standards.name: End-to-end uncertainty and significance
evidence_standards.detail: Each task-condition bar represents 600 calls (six LMs × 100 calls per LM); show 95% Wilson score confidence intervals and use a two-proportion z-test, with significance marked at p<0.05.

evidence_standards.name: Decoding and retry setting
evidence_standards.detail: For end-to-end agent calls, the Strands runtime retries until the output passes the post-condition or reaches a hard limit of five attempts.

datasets.name: 14 hand-designed structured-output tasks
datasets.eval_protocol: Five models were evaluated on 14 tasks spanning JSON generation (5), schema adherence (3), function calling (3), and extraction (3), under native, Outlines, and XGrammar decoding. Outputs were checked against each task’s JSON schema using Draft 2020-12; extraction content was scored against expected field values, and function calls by function selection and required-parameter presence. No split is specified.

baselines.name: native decoding
baselines.fair_comparison: Compared on the same five models and 14 tasks as the constrained conditions, using greedy decoding (T=0, do_sample=False).

baselines.name: Outlines
baselines.fair_comparison: Compared on the same five models and 14 tasks as the other decoding conditions, using greedy decoding (T=0, do_sample=False).

baselines.name: XGrammar
baselines.fair_comparison: Compared on the same five models and 14 tasks as the other decoding conditions, using greedy decoding (T=0, do_sample=False).

metrics.name: schema validity
metrics.caveat: Schema validity is necessary but not sufficient for semantic correctness; valid output can still omit task intent or contain poor-quality parameter values. The paper also reports content accuracy and function-call scores.

metrics.name: content accuracy
metrics.caveat: Exact matching can count formatting variants of semantically correct values as failures, so the paper normalizes case, whitespace, and formatting punctuation before comparison. The authors also note field-level matching is coarse.

metrics.name: function call score
metrics.caveat: The score gives credit for function selection and required-parameter presence, but parameter presence does not measure parameter quality; the paper illustrates this with an email body containing only a numbered list.

metrics.name: generation throughput
metrics.caveat: The paper notes that Qwen-4B’s reported 8% XGrammar throughput increase is within single-run variance.

controls.name: native decoding
controls.detail: The unmodified, unconstrained greedy-decoding condition (no logits processor), run alongside Outlines and XGrammar on the same models and tasks.
controls.rules_out: Provides a reference for the effect of adding constrained decoding, rather than attributing the constrained-condition results to model and task differences.

confounds.name: structural failures are an artifact of greedy decoding
confounds.detail: The headline structural-validity improvement could reflect the choice of deterministic greedy decoding rather than a stable failure pattern.
confounds.ruled_out_by: A temperature robustness probe using 3 temperatures and 3 samples per condition; the paper reports that baseline failures were stable across sampling conditions.

confounds.name: formatting variants are mistaken for semantic errors
confounds.detail: Exact-match scoring could count semantically correct extraction values with different formatting as failures.
confounds.ruled_out_by: The paper scores normalized strings after stripping case, whitespace, and formatting punctuation; it reports that this removed 10 false-positive semantic failures.

evidence_standards.name: greedy decoding for the main evaluations
evidence_standards.detail: All conditions use T=0 and do_sample=False for determinism and reproducibility; no statistical test or significance threshold is reported.

evidence_standards.name: temperature robustness probe
evidence_standards.detail: Phase 2 uses 3 temperatures and 3 samples per condition to check whether baseline failures persist beyond greedy decoding.

datasets.name: users
datasets.eval_protocol: Custom benchmark case for a simple tabular structure. Each of 21 models was run 10 times at temperature 0 (other parameters at provider defaults). Outputs were validated with Pydantic, canonicalized, and compared with gold JSON; failures could receive up to 3 repair attempts. No split is specified.

datasets.name: order
datasets.eval_protocol: Custom benchmark case for a nested structure with an array. Each of 21 models was run 10 times at temperature 0 (other parameters at provider defaults). Outputs were validated with Pydantic, canonicalized, and compared with gold JSON; failures could receive up to 3 repair attempts. No split is specified.

datasets.name: company
datasets.eval_protocol: Custom benchmark case for a department-and-employee hierarchy. Each of 21 models was run 10 times at temperature 0 (other parameters at provider defaults). Outputs were validated with Pydantic, canonicalized, and compared with gold JSON; failures could receive up to 3 repair attempts. No split is specified.

datasets.name: invoice
datasets.eval_protocol: Custom benchmark case for items and totals. Each of 21 models was run 10 times at temperature 0 (other parameters at provider defaults). Outputs were validated with Pydantic, canonicalized, and compared with gold JSON; failures could receive up to 3 repair attempts. No split is specified.

baselines.name: Plain JSON generation (J)
baselines.fair_comparison: Run on the same models, cases, and repetitions as the other tracks, at temperature 0 with other parameters at provider defaults; uses the shared JSON prompt with JSON-SO.

baselines.name: JSON Structured Output (JSO; constrained decoding)
baselines.fair_comparison: Run on the same models, cases, and repetitions as the other tracks, at temperature 0 with other parameters at provider defaults; uses the shared JSON prompt with plain JSON.

metrics.name: One-shot accuracy
metrics.caveat: Counts only cases correct on the first attempt, so it does not capture cases recovered by repair; the paper also reports final accuracy after repairs.

metrics.name: Final accuracy
metrics.caveat: Does not by itself reflect the token cost of repair cycles; the paper reports total token usage alongside it.

metrics.name: Token budget / token usage
metrics.caveat: Includes prompt and completion tokens, so instructional prompt overhead and repair cycles can offset output-token savings; the paper records prompt and completion usage and reports total consumption.

metrics.name: Token efficiency
metrics.caveat: Defined as final accuracy per 1,000 tokens; the grouped analysis averages cases equally to avoid domination by token-heavy cases, unlike the earlier aggregate table.

controls.name: Plain JSON generation (J), without constrained decoding
controls.detail: The same models are evaluated on the same cases using plain JSON alongside JSON-SO constrained decoding.
controls.rules_out: Provides an unconstrained reference for judging whether results differ when JSON constrained decoding is applied.

confounds.name: TOON token savings may be offset by instructional prompt overhead
confounds.detail: A lower-token output could appear efficient while the TOON instructions make the total prompt-plus-completion cost higher.
confounds.ruled_out_by: The paper records prompt and completion tokens and compares total token budgets across formats, including per-case token costs.

confounds.name: Repair cycles may account for token costs or final-accuracy differences
confounds.detail: A format that fails initially may recover after retries, while consuming additional tokens; final accuracy alone would not show that cost.
confounds.ruled_out_by: The paper reports one-shot and final accuracy separately and measures total token usage including repair cycles; it also discusses the invoice case’s repair-related token increase.

confounds.name: TOON’s results may depend on case structure rather than general format performance
confounds.detail: A headline result across cases could reflect the mix of TOON-aligned and non-aligned structures.
confounds.ruled_out_by: The paper reports case-level results and separately analyzes aligned cases (users, order, invoice) and the non-aligned company case.

evidence_standards.name: 10 repeated runs per model and test case at temperature 0
evidence_standards.detail: The paper averages run-level results by model and says repetitions were used to check output stability and consistency across API calls, not sampling variance. Other parameters were provider defaults. It reports no statistical test, confidence interval, or numerical margin for treating results as ties.

datasets.name: Spider
datasets.eval_protocol: Uses 100 unique schemas selected as the most question-rich, with up to 5 associated questions per schema. Each schema is mutated at minor (1–2 changes), moderate (3–5 changes), and major (5–8 changes) severity. Evaluates SQL generation, JSON generation using a JSON Schema derived from the first table, and record generation for a target table; prompts instruct models to use only the mutated schema. Aggregates at the schema level (100 schemas × 3 drift levels per model). No train/test split is specified. SQL is parsed with sqlglot and checked for table/column references in the mutated schema; JSON and records are checked with jsonschema, strict type checking, key-set comparison, cross-field relational checks, and structural-depth verification. Unparseable outputs are terminal failures; drift-induced fabrication is identified by comparison with the original schema.

datasets.name: Synthetic schemas
datasets.eval_protocol: Supplementary experiment on 20 schemas with randomized identifiers, used to probe Spider memorization. Reports hallucination rates across models and compares rates across drift severity; the drift curve is reported as remaining within 2 percentage points. No further split or scoring details are specified.

baselines.name: Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct
baselines.fair_comparison: Evaluated with the same zero-shot prompts and greedy decoding (temperature 0) as the other models. Runs locally with 4-bit NF4 quantization; the paper notes that local quantized models versus unquantized API models are not perfectly controlled.

baselines.name: Mistral-7B-Instruct-v0.3
baselines.fair_comparison: Evaluated with the same zero-shot prompts and greedy decoding (temperature 0) as the other models. Runs locally with 4-bit NF4 quantization; the paper notes that local quantized models versus unquantized API models are not perfectly controlled.

baselines.name: Gemini 2.5 Flash
baselines.fair_comparison: Evaluated with the same zero-shot prompts and greedy decoding (temperature 0) as the other models. Accessed through an API and unquantized; the paper notes that API models versus local 4-bit quantized models are not perfectly controlled.

baselines.name: Llama-3.3-70B (Groq API)
baselines.fair_comparison: Evaluated with the same zero-shot prompts and greedy decoding (temperature 0) as the other models. Accessed through an API and unquantized; the paper notes that API models versus local 4-bit quantized models are not perfectly controlled.

metrics.name: Parseability
metrics.caveat: High parseability does not imply semantic reliability; the paper reports semantic validity alongside it. Estimates were sensitive to handling array-wrapped outputs: Gemini Flash rose from about 65% in preliminary evaluation to 97.7% with proper array handling.

metrics.name: Schema validity
metrics.caveat: Schema validation alone misses semantic errors: 8.0% of outputs that pass formal JSON Schema validation still have semantic hallucinations, primarily type coercion and relational inconsistency.

metrics.name: Semantic validity
metrics.caveat: Cross-task comparisons are affected by evaluation strictness: SQL checks table and column reference validity, whereas JSON and record outputs receive the full taxonomy-based evaluation.

metrics.name: Hallucination rate
metrics.caveat: For Spider, possible memorization or contamination could explain the flat drift curve; the paper also reports a synthetic-schema experiment. Record-generation rates may reflect missing information as well as schema non-compliance, and should not be attributed solely to structured hallucination.

metrics.name: Hallucination-type prevalence (including semantic field confusion)
metrics.caveat: The semantic field confusion detector uses a heuristic that can flag legitimate numeric strings in text fields; the paper says its 0.7–7.3% rates should be treated as upper bounds. Relational checks also use domain-specific heuristics that may not generalize.

metrics.name: Drift-induced hallucination rate
metrics.caveat: Possible Spider memorization or contamination could make the drift results unrepresentative; synthetic schemas with randomized identifiers are also evaluated.

controls.name: Synthetic schemas with randomized identifiers
controls.detail: Runs a supplementary evaluation on 20 schemas with randomized identifiers unlikely to appear verbatim in pretraining, alongside the Spider-schema evaluation; reports hallucination rates of 40–58% across models and a drift curve within 2 percentage points across severity levels.
controls.rules_out: Provides evidence that the high hallucination rates and flat drift curve are not explained by Spider memorization alone; the paper cautions that the small-scale experiment does not definitively resolve memorization.

confounds.name: Spider schema memorization or benchmark contamination
confounds.detail: Models could recall public Spider schemas or outputs, making the flat drift curve appear even if they are not generally conditioning on the supplied schema.
confounds.ruled_out_by: Evaluates 20 synthetic schemas with randomized identifiers; hallucination rates remain high (40–58%) and the drift curve remains within 2 percentage points across severity levels. The paper says this is supporting evidence, not a definitive resolution.

confounds.name: Fixed zero-shot prompt design
confounds.detail: Observed schema-conditioning failures could result partly from prompt choices rather than intrinsic model limitations; few-shot, schema-highlighted, or self-check prompting might change the results.
confounds.ruled_out_by: Not ruled out: the paper does not ablate prompting strategies and identifies this as a limitation.

confounds.name: Quantization differences between local and API models
confounds.detail: Quality differences could be caused partly by 4-bit quantization of local models rather than model-specific behavior.
confounds.ruled_out_by: Not ruled out: the paper says a same-model quantized versus unquantized controlled comparison would be needed and does not provide one.

confounds.name: Missing information in record-generation prompts
confounds.detail: Low record-generation performance could reflect that Spider questions are queries about data, not text containing extractable values, rather than schema non-compliance alone.
confounds.ruled_out_by: Not separated: the paper explicitly says the low performance reflects a combination of missing information and schema non-compliance and should not be attributed solely to structured hallucination.

confounds.name: Evaluation strictness differs across output tasks
confounds.detail: Cross-task validity differences could partly reflect SQL being checked only for table/column references while JSON and records receive the full taxonomy-based checks.
confounds.ruled_out_by: Not ruled out: the paper acknowledges this asymmetry as a limitation on cross-task comparisons.

confounds.name: Formatting failures explain apparent semantic failures
confounds.detail: Unparseable outputs might contain recoverable semantic content, so counting them as failures could inflate apparent semantic failure.
confounds.ruled_out_by: Applies lightweight JSON repair to unparseable outputs; semantic validity improves by zero for every model.

confounds.name: Heuristic false positives in semantic field confusion detection
confounds.detail: Numeric strings in text-typed fields may be legitimate values, so the detector could overcount field-confusion hallucinations.
confounds.ruled_out_by: Not ruled out: the paper identifies the rates as upper bounds and says more precise detection would require domain-specific knowledge.

evidence_standards.name: Greedy decoding and deterministic evaluation
evidence_standards.detail: All models use greedy decoding (temperature 0); the evaluation is deterministic and does not use LLM-based judging.

evidence_standards.name: 95% bootstrap confidence intervals
evidence_standards.detail: Reports 95% bootstrap confidence intervals for hallucination rates using 10,000 resamples.

evidence_standards.name: Chi-squared test for drift-rate differences
evidence_standards.detail: Uses a chi-squared test for hallucination rates by drift severity; reports p = 0.59 and treats the minor-to-major difference as not statistically significant.

datasets.name: BIRD-SQL
datasets.eval_protocol: Evaluate on the Dev set. Synthetic setting: randomly split each schema’s labeled pairs into equal matched and unmatched halves; generate one synthetic NLQ-SQL pair with a different database literal for each matched pair, index the synthetic pairs, and evaluate on the original pairs (matched queries have a matching template). Non-synthetic setting: use recurring templates found in BIRD-dev and generated paraphrases to form the template bank; evaluate on 73 matching and an equal number of sampled non-matching queries (134 total). Score SQL with Execution Match Accuracy: whether predicted and gold SQL yield the same database execution results.

datasets.name: Spider
datasets.eval_protocol: Evaluate on the Dev set. Synthetic setting: randomly split each schema’s labeled pairs into equal matched and unmatched halves; generate one synthetic NLQ-SQL pair with a different database literal for each matched pair, index the synthetic pairs, and evaluate on the original pairs (matched queries have a matching template). Non-synthetic setting: use recurring templates found in Spider-dev and generated paraphrases to form the template bank; evaluate on 499 queries, 484 matching and 15 non-matching. Score SQL with Execution Match Accuracy: whether predicted and gold SQL yield the same database execution results.

datasets.name: Proprietary workload of a large bank
datasets.eval_protocol: Group workload queries by shared parametric SQL template and report the fraction of queries in templates of different sizes; use sequential arrival to estimate how many queries would have a previously observed matching template. The paper does not report a workload size.

baselines.name: ZeroShot
baselines.fair_comparison: Compared on the same benchmark sets and LLMs as the other generation methods; no in-context examples are provided.

baselines.name: ICL-3
baselines.fair_comparison: Compared on the same benchmark sets and LLMs as the other generation methods; uses three labeled Text-SQL pairs whose NLQs are most similar to the query.

baselines.name: Cosine-similarity template-matching baseline
baselines.fair_comparison: Evaluated on the same BIRD and Spider template-selection task; the cosine threshold is chosen on a sample with equal numbers of positive and negative examples to maximize the true-positive-rate minus false-positive-rate difference.

baselines.name: Unconstrained generation
baselines.fair_comparison: Compared on the same BIRD and Spider dev sets and LLMs as constrained decoding; generates SQL without template constraints.

metrics.name: Template selection accuracy
metrics.caveat: Selection accuracy alone does not capture rejection of queries with no matching template; the paper reports rejection accuracy and their average alongside it.

metrics.name: Template rejection accuracy
metrics.caveat: Rejection accuracy alone does not capture selection among queries that do have a matching template; the paper reports selection accuracy and their average alongside it.

metrics.name: Overall template-selection accuracy (average)
metrics.caveat: The average can conceal different performance on matched and unmatched queries; the paper also reports selection and rejection accuracy separately.

controls.name: TeCoD-SGC
controls.detail: Use TeCoD’s selected template as a soft instruction to the LLM, without hard grammar-constrained enforcement.
controls.rules_out: That gains over ICL come only from template selection or prompting with a template; comparison with hard-constrained TeCoD tests the contribution of strict enforcement.

controls.name: Unconstrained generation
controls.detail: Generate SQL with the same LLM without template constraints.
controls.rules_out: That the accuracy or latency results are simply properties of ordinary unconstrained generation.

controls.name: TeCoD without two-phase decoding
controls.detail: Use the flexible template grammar with the default whole-grammar constrained-decoding algorithm instead of partitioned decoding.
controls.rules_out: That TeCoD’s latency improvement is unrelated to its two-phase decoding strategy.

controls.name: TeCoD without context tokens
controls.detail: Omit the left and right boundary context tokens when generating literal slots.
controls.rules_out: That partitioned decoding’s accuracy is unaffected by tokenization across partition boundaries.

controls.name: Fixed Template (no context)
controls.detail: Use a fixed, string-based template grammar without left and right context tokens.
controls.rules_out: That the accuracy differences between fixed and flexible templates are explained only by the presence of boundary context.

controls.name: Fixed Template (left and right context)
controls.detail: Use a fixed, string-based template grammar while including left and right context tokens.
controls.rules_out: Provides a fixed-template comparison with context, allowing comparison with TeCoD’s flexible grammar under contextualized literal generation.

confounds.name: Synthetic augmentation makes the matched-query evaluation artificially favorable
confounds.detail: Synthetic query pairs may introduce bias or make matched queries easier, so headline gains on the synthetic setting might not hold for real benchmark queries.
confounds.ruled_out_by: Also evaluate with a non-synthesized template bank and test queries drawn from recurring queries in the BIRD and Spider dev sets.

confounds.name: Template use harms queries that have no matching template
confounds.detail: A wrongly selected template can force an incorrect SQL, so gains on matched queries could obscure degraded performance on unmatched queries.
confounds.ruled_out_by: Evaluate matched and unmatched queries separately and report accuracy for both; the paper reports a 3–7% accuracy drop for unmatched queries while matched-query gains improve the overall average.

confounds.name: Fixed-template gains depend on the exact SQL surface formatting
confounds.detail: A fixed template may work because its string formatting happens to match the LLM’s formatting preferences or the benchmark SQL, rather than because the method is robust to template form.
confounds.ruled_out_by: Perturb template formatting by changing case, pretty-formatting, and inserting random whitespace; report ExM for fixed templates and state that TeCoD’s flexible grammar is invariant to the template’s string form.

confounds.name: Template-matcher results reflect exposure to test databases during training
confounds.detail: If the matcher’s training and test queries came from the same databases, its accuracy could reflect database-specific leakage rather than generalization.
confounds.ruled_out_by: Train the matcher on BIRD training databases that are disjoint from the databases used for testing.

datasets.name: ASLG-PC12
datasets.eval_protocol: English-to-gloss generation; evaluate BLEU on the 2,000-example test set. Main results report mean ± standard deviation over 10 randomly sampled test sets with different random seeds. Prompts use 20 fixed few-shot examples and an input-specific subset of the gloss taxonomy precomputed before training.

datasets.name: Web of Science (WoS)
datasets.eval_protocol: Hierarchical classification as a JSON object with predicted domain and area labels; evaluate Hierarchical F1 on the 2,000-example test set. Main results report mean ± standard deviation over 10 randomly sampled test sets with different random seeds. Prompts use one fixed few-shot example.

datasets.name: CoNLL-2003
datasets.eval_protocol: Named-entity recognition as a structured JSON object with person, organization, location, and miscellaneous fields; evaluate micro-F1 on the 2,000-example test set. Main results report mean ± standard deviation over 10 randomly sampled test sets with different random seeds. metrics.caveat: The authors note that natural-language answers may introduce distractions and parsing errors, while constraining the answer space may improve classification. They use an LLM as a perfect text parser to reduce answer-extraction errors.

controls.detail: The model first answers in natural language and then converts that answer into the target format.

confounds.name: Answer-extraction or parsing errors cause the performance gap
confounds.detail: Structured outputs may be harder to parse, so apparent task-performance differences could instead reflect failures to extract the final answer.
confounds.ruled_out_by: The authors use an LLM prompted to extract final answers, measure parsing-error rates, and report that near-zero parsing errors can coexist with substantial score gaps. They also test a corrective reformatting prompt for outputs with parsing errors.

confounds.name: Prompt wording sensitivity explains the differences
confounds.detail: Small prompt variations could change performance independently of the format restriction being studied.
confounds.ruled_out_by: They evaluate nine prompt combinations for format-restricting instructions—three task descriptions crossed with JSON, XML, and YAML schemas—and three natural-language wording variations, reporting averages and standard deviations.

confounds.name: JSON-mode key ordering disrupts reasoning-before-answer behavior
confounds.detail: On Last Letter, GPT-3.5-Turbo JSON-mode responses put the answer key before the reasoning key, potentially prompting direct answering rather than chain-of-thought reasoning and explaining the score drop.
confounds.ruled_out_by: The authors inspect the responses and report that 100% of GPT-3.5-Turbo JSON-mode responses placed the answer key before the reasoning key; they do not report a separate intervention that rules out this explanation.

evidence_standards.name: Prompt-variation averages and standard deviations
evidence_standards.detail: For format-restricting instructions, results are averaged over nine prompt combinations (three task descriptions and three schemas: JSON, XML, YAML); natural-language prompting uses three wording variations. The paper reports standard deviations across these variations. It does not state a statistical test, seed count, or numerical margin for treating results as ties.

baselines.fair_comparison: Keyword-generation baseline results are copied from He (2021); the paper does not state additional controls for a fair comparison.

baselines.name: BART
baselines.fair_comparison: For entity-guided summarization, the paper reports both previously reported results and its own implementation; it does not specify further equalized settings.

baselines.name: CTRLSum
baselines.fair_comparison: For entity-guided summarization, the paper reports both previously reported results and its own implementation; it conditions on lexical constraints, as does AutoTemplate, but directly generates the summary rather than a template.

metrics.name: Success rate of lexical constraint satisfaction
metrics.caveat: For entity-guided summarization, the paper's protocol is stricter than prior studies: it requires all oracle entities to appear, rather than checking whether a single specified entity appears.

metrics.name: Micro-averaged sentence-level grammaticality accuracy
metrics.caveat: The paper uses a grammatical acceptability classifier rather than external-language-model perplexity, noting that perplexity can assign low values to unnatural text containing common words.

controls.name: AutoTemplate with random initialization
controls.detail: The T5-based model is randomly initialized instead of using T5 pretraining.
controls.rules_out: A comparison against this ablation tests whether the reported text-quality results can be attributed to pretraining alone; the paper reports lower quality with random initialization.

controls.name: AutoTemplate with a single placeholder type
controls.detail: Uses <X> for all placeholders instead of unique placeholders ordered by appearance.
controls.rules_out: A comparison against this ablation tests whether unique placeholder tokens matter; the paper reports lower text quality with a single placeholder type.

confounds.name: Template generation could make the final output less fluent
confounds.detail: The template-generation step produces text with placeholders, which could leave the lexicalized output less fluent than directly generated text.
confounds.ruled_out_by: Compares grammatical-acceptability classifier micro-averaged sentence-level accuracy for AutoTemplate and baselines.

confounds.name: The summarization results may not establish faithfulness
confounds.detail: The authors acknowledge that automatic evaluation scores and satisfying oracle entity constraints do not guarantee that generated summaries are faithful to the source.
confounds.ruled_out_by: Not ruled out: the paper says the risk of unfaithful text remains and reports that it did not use LLM-as-a-judge or human evaluation.

evidence_standards.name: Regular beam search decoding
evidence_standards.detail: The template-generation model uses regular beam search; the paper does not specify a beam size or report seed counts, variance, confidence intervals, or statistical tests.

evidence_standards.name: Keyword-generation aggregation
evidence_standards.detail: Reports averaged performance across the number of keywords; no statistical significance rule or variance estimate is stated.

datasets.name: One-Billion-Word
datasets.eval_protocol: Filter sentences to lengths 10–40; use 1M sentences for training and 0.1M for validation. Construct six test sets of 1K sentences each using 1–6 keywords per sentence. Results for most models are averaged over the six constraint counts; sep-B/F and asyn-B/F results use only the one-constraint test set.

datasets.name: Yelp
datasets.eval_protocol: Filter sentences to lengths 10–40; use 1M sentences for training and 0.1M for validation. Construct six test sets of 1K sentences each using 1–6 keywords per sentence. Results for most models are averaged over the six constraint counts; sep-B/F and asyn-B/F results use only the one-constraint test set.

baselines.name: sep-B/F
baselines.fair_comparison: The traditional baselines, including sep-B/F, use GPT-2 small (12 layers, 12 heads, hidden size 768, 117M parameters); no further equality is stated.

baselines.name: asyn-B/F
baselines.fair_comparison: The traditional baselines, including asyn-B/F, use GPT-2 small (12 layers, 12 heads, hidden size 768, 117M parameters); no further equality is stated.

baselines.name: GBS
baselines.fair_comparison: The traditional baselines, including GBS, use GPT-2 small (12 layers, 12 heads, hidden size 768, 117M parameters); no further equality is stated.

baselines.name: CGMH
baselines.fair_comparison: The implemented GPT-2-small baselines use 12 layers, 12 heads, hidden size 768, and 117M parameters; CGMH is run for 200 refinement steps and its lowest-NLL candidate is selected.

baselines.name: X-MCMC-C
baselines.fair_comparison: Trained using the authors’ released code with XLNet-base-cased (12 layers, 12 heads, hidden size 768, 110M parameters); run for 200 refinement steps and select the lowest-NLL candidate.

baselines.name: POINTER
baselines.fair_comparison: Trained using released code and initialized with BERT-large; the POINTER models have 24 layers, 16 heads, hidden size 1024, and 336M parameters, described as comparable in parameter count to CBART.

baselines.name: POINTER-2
baselines.fair_comparison: Initialized with the general model pre-trained on English Wikipedia and has the same stated 336M-parameter configuration as POINTER. The paper explicitly notes this extra pretraining makes comparison with other models unfair.

metrics.name: BLEU (B-2, B-4)
metrics.caveat: Used as a measure of similarity between generated text and human references; no further caveat is stated.

metrics.name: NIST (N-2, N-4)
metrics.caveat: Used as a measure of similarity between generated text and human references; no further caveat is stated.

metrics.name: METEOR
metrics.caveat: Used as a measure of similarity between generated text and human references; no further caveat is stated.

metrics.name: Self-BLEU (SB-4)
metrics.caveat: Measures similarity among generations; lower values indicate greater diversity. No further caveat is stated.

metrics.name: Distinct n-grams (D-2, D-4)
metrics.caveat: Counts unique bigrams or 4-grams divided by total generated tokens; higher values indicate greater diversity. No further caveat is stated.

metrics.name: Sentence-level n-gram repetitions (Rep)
metrics.caveat: Counts a sentence as repetitive if a unigram occurs more than twice or a trigram more than once within its first 20 tokens.

metrics.name: Latency (La)
metrics.caveat: Average decoding time per sentence on test sets without mini-batching.

metrics.name: Human fluency preference
metrics.caveat: Pairwise judgments allow ties; three volunteers evaluate sampled sentences. No further caveat is stated.

metrics.name: Human informativeness preference
metrics.caveat: Pairwise judgments allow ties; three volunteers evaluate sampled sentences. No further caveat is stated.

metrics.name: Fleiss’ kappa
metrics.caveat: Reported as inter-rater agreement for the fluency and informativeness judgments.

controls.name: CBART without repetition penalty
controls.detail: Ablation removes the repetition penalty (Table 4, row 6), compared with the standard CBART condition.
controls.rules_out: The observed reduction in repetitions is not attributable merely to running CBART; the comparison tests the contribution of the repetition penalty.

controls.name: CBART trained with MLM instead of LM
controls.detail: The decoder predicts only masked tokens rather than reconstructing the original text (Table 5, row 2).
controls.rules_out: The results are not explained simply by using CBART regardless of its training objective; this tests the stated LM objective against MLM.

controls.name: CBART without causal attention mask
controls.detail: The causal attention mask is removed from the decoder (Table 5, row 3; also an MLM-without-mask variant in row 4).
controls.rules_out: Tests whether the causal attention mask is responsible for CBART’s results.

controls.name: CBART with random initialization
controls.detail: A six-layer CBART model is initialized with random values rather than pretrained weights (Table 5, row 5).
controls.rules_out: Tests whether the results are explained by the proposed architecture alone rather than pretraining.

controls.name: CBART initialized with BART-base
controls.detail: A base CBART model initialized with BART-base is compared with the large CBART model initialized with BART-large (Table 5, rows 6–7).
controls.rules_out: Tests whether model size and pretrained checkpoint account for performance differences.

confounds.name: More lexical constraints make reference-like generation easier
confounds.detail: The authors note that increasing constraints shrinks the solution space, which can itself increase BLEU, NIST, and METEOR without demonstrating a general improvement in generation.
confounds.ruled_out_by: They report results separately for constraint counts N=1–6 and explicitly attribute the quality increase in part to the smaller solution space; this explanation is not ruled out.

confounds.name: Pretraining and model size, rather than the proposed design, explain performance
confounds.detail: The authors state that pretrained models and model size matter, so gains over smaller or randomly initialized systems could reflect those factors.
confounds.ruled_out_by: They compare random initialization, BART-base, and BART-large variants on Yelp, but these comparisons do not isolate all architectural contributions.

confounds.name: Low NLL need not mean fluent, high-quality text
confounds.detail: The paper notes that language models can assign low NLL to repetitive or generic sentences, so a low NLL could produce an apparently favorable fluency assessment without better text.
confounds.ruled_out_by: NLL is not used as a sentence-fluency metric; the paper reports quality and diversity metrics and conducts a human fluency evaluation.

evidence_standards.name: Human pairwise evaluation
evidence_standards.detail: For each compared model, randomly select 50 sentences; three independent volunteers with bachelor’s or higher degrees compare sentence pairs for fluency or informativeness, with ties allowed. Pair order is shuffled. Report preference percentages and Fleiss’ kappa (0.69 for fluency, 0.65 for informativeness), described as substantial agreement. No statistical significance test or multi-seed procedure is stated.

evidence_standards.name: Reported decoding settings
evidence_standards.detail: Baselines sep-B/F, asyn-B/F, and GBS use beam width 5; CGMH and X-MCMC-C use 200 refinement steps and select the lowest-NLL candidate; POINTER uses greedy decoding. CBART results include greedy and top-k/top-p settings, with multiple-sequence decoding using the stated sequence count. Latency is measured without mini-batching.
